lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- She Said, He Asked
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Bruna Viana da Silva Rocha | Lesson 9 -- She Said, He Asked

listenings.text: I run training sessions on this and I always start with the same number. A message that goes through four people loses about half of what it was. Not the words. The words survive. What dies is the part that tells you what to do with it. Somebody said the meeting had been moved, and by the fourth person that had become the meeting was canceled, and nobody in that chain lied. Here is the thing I actually teach. When you pass something on, you have to carry two pieces. What was said, and who said it. People drop the second one first, every single time, because it feels like a detail. It is not a detail. It is the whole difference between she told me the gate had changed and apparently the gate changed. One of those you can act on. The other one is weather. So when somebody tells you something that matters, ask one question before you walk away. Ask who told them.

I want to explain something, because people get angry at me and I understand it, but I am the last person in the chain, not the first. A gate change is decided somewhere else, by somebody who is looking at forty-one aircraft and not at you. I am told about it, usually, between four and nine minutes before you are. Sometimes I find out because the board changes and I turn around and look at it like everybody else. So here is my honest advice, and I am not supposed to give it. Do not ask me if the gate is going to change, because I will tell you what I was told, and what I was told is already old. Ask me a different question. Ask me how far the new gate would be if it did change. I can answer that one, and it is the only thing that is actually going to help you, because in this airport the answer is sometimes four minutes and sometimes twenty-six.
